newsitem.title: JAPAN: No breakthrough soon on WTO/China - Japan official.
newsitem.headline: No breakthrough soon on WTO/China - Japan official.

text.p: World Trade Organisation (WTO) members want China to join the global trade body as soon as possible, but no breakthrough in talks on the topic is likely soon, a Japanese diplomat said on Monday.
"There is a common feeling among negotiators...that the Chinese economy is changing rapidly day by day and at some stage we have to...conclude the negotiations," the official told Reuters.
The United States, long at odds with Beijing over conditions for China's entry into the WTO, wants to see the talks wrapped up "in a fairly limited time," he said.
But he added, "The fundamental thing remains unchanged -- that they have not changed the criteria for accession."

A former U.S. trade official said here last week that Washington was eager to break the impasse over China's entry into the WTO and had signalled the change in its appointment of China specialist Lee Sands as U.S. negotiator on the issue.

The Japanese official said Chinese trade officials had interpreted the appointment of Sands, an experienced negotiator with Beijing, as a sign Washington would take a more pragmatic approach in the talks.
"Chinese negotiators do think he understands China better and would adopt a more pragmatic approach," the official said.

Chinese Vice Trade Minister Long Yongtu, here last week for a seminar on the subject of Beijing's entry into the WTO, said the atmosphere surrounding the talks had improved but added China would reject any conditions it saw as too strict.

Beijing has sought admission under more lenient standards set for developing nations, while Washington wants China to meet stricter standards to more advanced economies, taking its huge size into account.

China also wants assurances that its concessions would be matched by a U.S. move to make Beijing's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) status permanent instead of subject to an annual review, the Japanese official said.
MFN, granted to almost all major U.S. trading partners, allows the importation of goods at much lower tariffs.
The lack of consensus inside China on the merits of speedy accession to the WTO, which would entail high costs to domestic industries, remains a big barrier to concluding the talks.

"There is still a sense in China that they can do business without the WTO and continue to do it in a way that they want...and that joining the WTO would mean sacrificing some of their domestic industries and vested interests," he said.

No major breakthrough is expected at working-level talks later this week in Geneva, nor is China's WTO membership likely to be a major issue on the agenda at WTO ministerial meetings in Singapore in December, the Japanese official said.
